analysis_claims.universe: All eligible households; each distribution uses its own valid 1–5 responses. A2 retains original wording and coding.
analysis_claims.weighting: wt_final; fixed synthetic target profile; valid-case percentages transcribed from supplied tables.

analysis_claims.universe: Membership requires agreement on both valid defining attitudes: budget A3/A4, effort A5/A6, waste A7/A8. Both must be valid to classify nonmembership. Joint membership requires all three flags valid; unknown is not absence of need.
analysis_claims.weighting: wt_final; original fixed-profile weights. Joint summaries use supplied unrounded membership percentages.

analysis_claims.universe: Current use: valid U1 among all eligible households. Satisfaction and sharing: valid follow-up answers among recorded current users only. U1 DK/refusal split is unavailable in supplied tables.
analysis_claims.weighting: wt_final; fixed synthetic target profile; separate valid-case denominators for U1, U2 and U3.

analysis_claims.universe: Valid A9 responses within responding-planner age bands; age is complete and describes the planner, not every household member.
analysis_claims.weighting: wt_final; original fixed-profile weights within each age group; descriptive comparisons only.

analysis_claims.universe: Valid corresponding need state and answered N1 block, including all-zero None responses. Full eligible state bases are restored from the matching external-outcome tables; subgroup block nonresponse is eligible minus answered n. Its DK/refusal split is unavailable.
analysis_claims.weighting: wt_final; weighted respondent incidence using original fixed-profile weights. Descriptive differences from supplied tables; no additional significance tests.

findings.proposition: Pilot quick meals and flexible replanning alongside use-up and budget help: requests are 60.82%, 59.16% and 57.12%, respectively. Sharing attracts 47.23%. The evidence supports a task shortlist, not a proven winner.
findings.claim_strength: Descriptive evidence supporting a pilot recommendation
findings.qualification: Eligible N/weighted N=2700/2700; answered n/weighted n/ESS=2596/2595.96/2045.54 for every item. DK=80, refusal=24; 116 all-zero None respondents remain included. Structural omissions=0. These are multiple-response respondent incidences. The three leading tasks differ by at most 3.70 points; sharing is descriptively 9.88–13.59 points lower, exceeding the 8-point attention threshold. No paired superiority test is supplied, and task requests do not establish digital-product demand.

findings.proposition: Recruit households meeting the effort criteria as a priority pilot audience. They report 2.19 versus 0.97 top-up days in the past seven days: +1.22 days (95% CI 1.10 to 1.34; Holm p=3.72e-84). They report 3.73 versus 4.93 days with the evening meal decided by the previous evening: −1.20 days (CI −1.36 to −1.04; Holm p=3.28e-48). Both exceed the 0.5-day attention threshold.
findings.claim_strength: Prespecified associations with Holm-adjusted p-values; recruitment recommendation
findings.qualification: Group order is criteria met/not met. Eligible N/weighted N=904/809.73 and 1642/1729.28. Top-ups valid n/weighted n/ESS=878/782.55/661.07 and 1588/1669.18/1286.98; DK/refusal=18/8 and 42/12. Planning valid bases=872/779.09/656.41 and 1586/1666.86/1285.52; DK/refusal=22/10 and 40/16. Unknown effort state=154; structural omissions=0. These are weighted associations, not covariate-adjusted causal effects or proof that this audience is commercially superior.

findings.proposition: Include budget and waste needs in recruitment. Budget-state households report overspending in at least one of four weeks at 72.31% versus 35.03%: +37.28 points (95% CI 32.70 to 41.86; Holm p=9.69e-57). Waste-state households report 1.87 versus 0.87 discard days in seven: +1.00 day (CI 0.87 to 1.14; Holm p=1.04e-47). Both exceed their attention thresholds.
findings.qualification: Budget met/not-met eligible N/weighted N=717/667.29 and 1840/1896.95; valid n/weighted n/ESS=678/631.58/522.17 and 1708/1769.77/1368.26; DK/refusal=33/6 and 107/25; unknown state=143. Waste eligible bases=821/775.51 and 1728/1785.80; valid bases=797/754.72/615.00 and 1664/1721.13/1331.13; DK/refusal=14/10 and 41/23; unknown state=151. Structural omissions=0. Overspending measures incidence, not money; discard measures days, not quantity. Separate within-state contrasts cannot rank overlapping need states or predict intervention benefits.

findings.proposition: Match pilot tasks to expressed needs without restricting access to the defined states. Budget help is requested by 78.13% meeting budget criteria versus 50.03% not meeting them (+28.10 points); use-up help by 73.61% meeting waste criteria versus 53.23% not meeting them (+20.38 points). Both descriptive gaps exceed 8 points, while substantial requests remain outside each state.
findings.qualification: Eligible and answered bases, ESS and unknown-state counts are retained in analysis_claims.support_requests_by_corresponding_need. Budget answered n=680/1784; waste answered n=786/1666, in met/not-met order. Subgroup block nonresponse totals are recoverable, but DK/refusal splits are not. No confirmatory tests are supplied for these contrasts. Requests and defining attitudes concern related topics; this is not independent validation, uptake evidence or proof of exclusive audience fit.

findings.proposition: Recruit overlapping needs rather than exclusive personas. Effort, waste and budget criteria are met by 31.89%, 30.28% and 26.02% of their respective derivable bases. Among households with all flags valid, 58.89% meet at least one state, 24.44% meet at least two, and 5.93% meet all three.
findings.qualification: Eligible N/weighted N=2700/2700. Full bases, unknown counts and all eight combinations are retained in analysis_claims.need_state_sizes_and_joint_membership. Joint valid n/weighted n/ESS=2280/2290.14/1799.62; 420 lack at least one flag. Marginal prevalence uses different valid denominators. Numerical prevalence differences do not establish superiority; meeting no defined state does not mean having no support needs.

findings.proposition: Include households with children under 16 as a practical recruitment context. They report 1.91 versus 1.17 top-up days: +0.73 day (95% CI 0.63 to 0.84; Holm p=3.91e-40), exceeding the attention threshold. Their planning difference is smaller: 4.23 versus 4.64 days, −0.40 day (CI −0.54 to −0.27; Holm p=6.64e-9), statistically detectable but below the 0.5-day point-estimate threshold.
findings.claim_strength: Prespecified household-context associations with Holm-adjusted p-values
findings.qualification: Children/no-children eligible N/weighted N=1296/702 and 1404/1998. Top-ups valid n/weighted n/ESS=1258/681.17/1216.30 and 1356/1926.49/1273.98; DK/refusal=29/9 and 36/12. Planning valid bases=1254/679.47/1212.62 and 1355/1923.93/1272.60; DK/refusal=30/12 and 35/14. Unknown children status and structural omissions=0. Planning's interval includes magnitudes above 0.5 day. Children status is neither a need definition nor a causal explanation. Differences use unrounded estimates.

findings.proposition: Keep participation optional and test delivery format across ages. Digital receptivity is polarised: 46.82% agree, 47.38% disagree and 5.80% are neutral; strong agreement and strong disagreement are each about 35%. Agreement is descriptively lower among planners aged 65+ (37.49%) than in each younger band (48.77–51.22%), so an overall average could hide recruitment and accessibility challenges.
findings.claim_strength: Descriptive overall distribution and age differences
findings.qualification: Overall eligible N/weighted N=2700/2700; valid n/weighted n/ESS=2610/2609.19/2057.46; DK=67, refusal=23, structural omissions=0. Full overall and age distributions and bases appear in analysis_claims.ordinal_distributions and digital_receptivity_by_age. Age differences exceed the 8-point attention threshold descriptively; no age significance tests or adjustment for other characteristics are supplied. Age describes the responding planner. This general attitude is not concept acceptance, an uptake forecast or grounds to exclude older households.

findings.proposition: Existing tools provide useful comparison experiences, but the study does not establish a dissatisfied replacement market. Current use is 38.90% among valid household screeners. Among valid current-user follow-ups, 83.15% are satisfied and 54.27% have used sharing.
findings.claim_strength: Descriptive prevalence and conditional user experience
findings.qualification: Routing, full satisfaction distribution and eligible/valid bases with ESS appear in analysis_claims.tool_routing_and_satisfaction. Satisfaction and sharing apply only to answering current users. Follow-ups are unasked for 1595 known nonusers and 65 unknown screeners; the latter's DK/refusal split is unavailable. Current users are selected; satisfaction does not establish effectiveness or retained use. Older paid-user satisfaction remains suppressed: eligible N/weighted N=20/20.36; valid n/weighted n/ESS=18/18.27/17.73; DK=2, refusal=0. This subgroup also falls below the ESS warning threshold.

findings.proposition: Test flexibility, low setup effort, acceptable cost and information-sharing controls together. Barriers are tightly grouped: rigidity 49.56%, extra cost 49.56%, privacy 48.72% and setup/upkeep 47.90%. Compare realistic delivery alternatives on task completion and burden; obtain price evidence, observed uptake, repeated use and controlled outcome evidence before commercial claims.
findings.claim_strength: Descriptive barriers and evidence-informed research recommendation
findings.qualification: Eligible N/weighted N=2700/2700; answered n/weighted n/ESS=2570/2574.37/2029.07 for every barrier; DK=101, refusal=29, structural omissions=0. Includes 204 None respondents; multiple selections permitted. Largest barrier gap is 1.66 points, below the 8-point attention threshold; no winner or equivalence is established. Follow-up research has not been conducted. The study provides no randomised concept exposure, price test, observed purchase, revenue or longitudinal retention evidence.

beats.headline_intent: Pilot flexible meal help with use-up and budget tasks, recruiting households with relevant difficulties
beats.analytical_relationship: Broad requests define the task shortlist; prespecified external-outcome contrasts identify relevant difficulties; descriptive task requests strengthen budget and waste audience fit without proving uptake or intervention effects.

beats.headline_intent: Recruit across overlapping needs and household contexts without making state membership an access rule
beats.analytical_relationship: Joint membership rules out exclusive personas, children status adds a practical context, and requests outside the defined states argue against restricting eligibility.

beats.headline_intent: Keep support optional and test delivery across ages and existing tool experience
beats.analytical_relationship: Polarised receptivity and descriptive age differences qualify task demand; conditional satisfaction cautions against assuming current users want a replacement.

beats.headline_intent: Use the pilot to resolve usability, adoption and value questions
beats.analytical_relationship: Closely grouped barriers define design questions. Observed behaviour, repeated use, price research and controlled outcomes are needed to progress from a task shortlist to format selection and commercial claims.

method_notes: Reviewed only the supplied brief, questionnaire, codebook and analysis tables in the prompt. No tools, external sources, file discovery, delegated agents or raw-data analyses were used. analysis_claims are rounded table transcriptions and explicit arithmetic summaries.

Change log: preserved the eight original findings and all six required contrasts; clarified the F1 task-to-percentage mapping and the descriptive sharing gap; replaced ambiguous 'adjusted associations' wording with explicit Holm-adjusted p-values; added material task–audience alignment as F9 and age receptivity context within F6. Retained routing, overlap, suppression and causal qualifications.

All households and targets are fictional. The 2700-household sample uses eight disproportionate age-by-children quota strata. wt_final standardises to a fixed synthetic profile; weighted N is an equivalent sample count, not UK population size. Results cannot establish real UK prevalence.

Every reported estimate uses its relevant valid-case denominator. Unknown derived states, DK, refusals and unasked follow-ups remain distinct. Some tables label prefiltered valid domains as eligible; full eligibility is restored where recoverable. Unavailable U1 and subgroup support-block DK/refusal splits are null, not zero.

Full weighted distributions are retained for all nine attitude items and current-user satisfaction, plus the age-specific attitude estimates used in F6. Codes 97/98 are excluded. Only A2 is reversed when computing the planning-orientation index; all item distributions preserve original coding. No index result is needed for the pilot recommendation.

All six required contrasts retain supplied inference: fixed-weight stratified domain-ratio linearisation across eight strata, all sampled rows retained with zero influence outside valid domains, and no finite-population correction. Holm adjustment applies separately to four needs_external and two household_context tests. Normal 95% intervals are unadjusted, not simultaneous. No additional confirmatory tests were introduced.

Kish ESS summarises weight dispersion and is not substituted for a variance estimator. Inference is conditional on observed valid responses and the fixed synthetic profile; it does not remove nonresponse bias, selection or causal uncertainty. Weighting and multiplicity adjustment do not constitute covariate-adjusted causal analysis.

The 0.5-day and 8-percentage-point thresholds guide pilot attention, not economic value. B1–B3 count days in the past seven, including valid zeroes; they do not count shops, meals, quantities or money. Small numerical gaps establish neither superiority nor equivalence.

Valid n below 40 requires suppression; n=40–74 requires a small-base warning; Kish ESS below 50 requires a warning. Older paid-user satisfaction remains suppressed, with no estimate inferred. No added finding relies on small-base evidence.

Remaining limits: these are cross-sectional self-reports without tested concepts, prices, observed purchase, revenue or retention. Task requests and related attitudes are not independent corroboration. Demographic differences are descriptive and potentially confounded. The revised narrative supports pilot research choices, not a selected commercial format or validated business impact.
